title: Randomize the sharer's attributes, with a behavioural share
rationale: In the source study close ties (+3.0 points, CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust (+5.7 points, CI [2.3, 9.1]) were associated with more sharing, but these attributes were respondents' ratings of real contacts and so bundle correlated traits. Randomizing tie and trust in a forwarded-post vignette tests whether they cause sharing of false headlines (misinformation was shared 18.2 points less than true headlines).
contribution: Turns descriptive tie-strength and trust contrasts into causal estimates, using a behavioural share outcome and a real-contact benchmark.
limitations: Vignette sharers are fictional, so the effects may differ from those for real contacts.
The mock-feed share is a behavioural proxy and not a real platform share.
The 2000 per arm target is for a 0.03 effect, so smaller interaction effects will be underpowered.

design.title: Randomized sharer tie and trust in forwarded posts
design.overview: Respondents consent, then see forwarded posts. Headline type (true, false, fact-check) is randomized between respondents. Within each respondent, tie strength (close or distant) and trust (high or low) are randomized across two forwarded-post vignettes. Respondents choose whether to share each post to a mock feed and rate its plausibility. A final block shows a post attributed to the respondent's own real contact as a benchmark.
design.hypothesis: H1: a randomized close tie raises the probability of sharing by about 0.03. H2: randomized high trust raises it by about 0.05. Both effects hold for false headlines.
design.primaryOutcome: Share of the forwarded post to the mock feed (binary).
design.comparison: Close vs distant tie and high vs low trust, within headline type. Standard errors are clustered by respondent. Headline type is a between-subject factor.
design.population: US adults from a YouGov-type online panel.

questions.text: You are invited to a research survey about how people share news online. It takes about 10 minutes and is voluntary. Do you agree to take part?

Imagine you receive a forwarded post in a messaging app. The sender is described as {{ed:tie1}} and as someone you {{ed:trust1}}. The post reads: "City council approves new budget for road repairs after public hearing."

Imagine you receive a forwarded post in a messaging app. The sender is described as {{ed:tie1}} and as someone you {{ed:trust1}}. The post reads: "Doctors admit common vaccine contains hidden tracking chips."

Imagine you receive a forwarded post in a messaging app. The sender is described as {{ed:tie1}} and as someone you {{ed:trust1}}. The post reads: "Fact-check: claim that vaccines contain tracking chips is false."
Would you share this post to your mock feed?
Based on the available information, do you think this post is more likely to be accurate or inaccurate?
Think of someone you discuss important matters with. Using initials only, enter who it is.
If this person forwarded you the same post, would you share it to your mock feed?
Thank you. Some posts were false and the senders were fictional. No post was actually shared. Please do not spread the false claims.

assumptions: Power target: about 2000 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (source H2 close tie 0.030 vs MDE 0.0258; H5 high trust 0.057 vs MDE 0.051).
Tie and trust levels are crossed and randomized by the survey platform in each vignette; the flow shows one fixed example per arm.
Platform is a YouGov-type US panel, with standard errors clustered by respondent.
Each respondent sees two vignettes, so the analysis clusters on respondent.
unresolved: The platform's randomization of tie and trust within each arm, the mock feed implementation, compensation and IRB number must be supplied by the research team.

evidence.title: Source study
evidence.claim: Close ties (+3.0) and high trust (+5.7) were associated with more sharing but were not randomized.
